references.text: God announces that He will wipe out the humans He has created from the face of the earth, along with the animals - this promise is fulfilled in 7:23.
The psalm calls for praising the Lord and expresses a desire that sinners should vanish from the earth, similar to how God wiped out all living things in the flood.
Jeremiah describes an earth that is desolate and empty without people or birds, a parallel to the total destruction in the flood.
Jesus refers to Noah's days when the flood came and took them all away, as a warning about the coming of the Son of Man.
By faith Noah built an ark for the salvation of his household after being warned about what had not yet been seen, and by this faith the world was condemned.
Peter mentions that in Noah's days eight souls were saved through water while waiting in the ark, a direct reference to only Noah and his family surviving the flood.
God did not spare the ancient world but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, along with seven others when He brought the flood upon the ungodly.
God promises never again to destroy all living things with a flood, a promise given after the total destruction described in 7:23.
Complementary descriptions of creation before and after judgment: destruction versus restoration.
Theological contrast between God's judgment (destruction) and His grace (to remember and save).
The same list of creatures links the judgment in 7:23 with the validity of the covenant in 9:10.
Parallel account of judgment: The earth closes over the guilty and wipes them out from society.
Jesus directly quoted the flood narrative as a picture of the coming judgment.
Theological principle: The righteous are saved while the ungodly are destroyed.
